extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants and practitioners evaluating §101 eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the two-part Alice/Mayo patent-eligibility framework, including considerations of improvements to technology, use of a particular machine, particular transformations, and whether additional elements are well‑understood, routine, and conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to existing technology (improvement consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention provides an improvement to an existing technological process; an improvement to technology weighs in favor of eligibility, regardless of the field of technology. An improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., an improvement to a fundamental economic concept) is not an improvement in technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claim describes a specific way the invention solves a technological problem (e.g., McRO: particular rules to set morph weights/phoneme transitions). Examples courts found sufficient to show improvement include: (i) a particular computerized method for operating a rubber molding press (Diamond v. Diehr); (ii) new telephone/server combinations (TLI Communications); (iii) advances in downloading/streaming (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV); (iv) improved digital data compression (DDR Holdings); (v) particular methods for virus screening on the Internet (Symantec); (vi) components/techniques that generate new data (Electric Power Group v. Alstom); (vii) specific inertial sensor configurations (Thales Visionix); (viii) a structured GUI that improves trader accuracy (Trading Techs. Int'l v. CQG); (ix) improved hepatocyte preservation (Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect). Examples courts found insufficient include commonplace business methods on a general-purpose computer (Alice), using well-known lab techniques to detect enzyme levels (Cleveland Clinic), gathering/analyzing information with conventional techniques and merely displaying it (TLI), delivering broadcast content at a high level of generality (Affinity Labs), general email screening on a generic computer (Symantec), and selecting generic content or functions from existing ranges (Affinity Labs). Keep in mind: the improvement must be to technology (computers, machines, physical processes), not merely an improved abstract idea or business process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite how computer aids the method (more than generic computer elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that a computer aids in improving technology, claims must recite details about how a computer aids the method, the extent to which it aids the method, or the significance of the computer to performance of the method; merely adding generic computer components is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim includes more than instructions to perform the method on generic components or machinery. If applicant adds a generic computer or generic computer components (including assertions of 'specially programmed' generic computers), the examiner should determine whether those added elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Mere recitation of a generic computer or conventional computer functions does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection. See MPEP §2106.05(f) for more on mere instructions to apply an exception. Cases: Alappat (superseded rationale that programming a generic computer renders eligibility); Alice Corp. (mere use of computer to perform existing process insufficient); Ultramercial and TLI (mere recitation of tangible components not necessarily inventive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration — particularity or generality of machine elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether a claim integrates a judicial exception via a particular machine (Step 2A Prong Two / Step 2B), consider the particularity or generality of the elements of the machine or apparatus; i.e., how specifically the machine can be identified rather than claiming 'any and all machines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that recites a machine with specific, identifiable structure (shape, conductors, components, arrangement) is more likely to integrate an exception into a practical application. Examples: Mackay Radio (specific antenna shape/arrangement), Eibel Process (Fourdrinier machine with defined structure). In contrast, a general-purpose computer that merely applies a judicial exception using conventional computer functions does not qualify as a 'particular machine.' See Ultramercial, TLI, Eon, and the discussion that Alappat's rationale is superseded by Bilski/Alice. Use this factor alongside other considerations (mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration — whether the machine implements the method steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the recited machine or apparatus actually implements the claimed method steps (plays an integral role) versus merely being an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the machine plays a significant part in permitting performance of the claimed method, it may integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. If the machine only functions as an obvious mechanism to achieve the solution more quickly or merely hosts the steps, it will likely not add significantly more. Example: CyberSource v. Retail Decisions — the Internet was not deemed to perform the fraud detection steps. See MPEP §2106.05(f) and case law (Versata) for when a machine must 'play a significant part' rather than being a mere tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration — whether involvement is extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which the machine's involvement imposes meaningful limits on the claim as opposed to being extra-solution activity or a mere field-of-use limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the machine contributes only nominally or insignificantly to executing the claimed method (e.g., limited to data-gathering steps or merely describing the source of data), it will not integrate the exception or provide significantly more. Cases: Bilski (field-of-use limitations insufficient), CyberSource (data-gathering steps insufficient). See MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test — useful clue but not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue and investigative tool for determining patent eligibility but is not a stand-alone test; claims must still be evaluated under the Alice/Mayo two-part framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that passes the Alice/Mayo test is eligible even if it fails the M-or-T test. Conversely, a claim that fails Alice/Mayo is ineligible even if it satisfies the M-or-T test. Use the M-or-T test alongside other considerations (mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use) to inform the analysis. See Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings, and Diehr discussions in MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation consideration (transformation of a particular article)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; such a transformation is a clue to patentability for process claims that do not include particular machines, though it is not a stand-alone test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'article' includes a physical object or substance that must be particular (specifically identifiable). 'Transformation' means the article has changed to a different state or thing — usually more than simply using the article or changing its location; a new/different function or use is evidence of transformation. Purely mental processes or mere manipulation of abstract data typically are not eligible transformations. Example: Tilghman v. Proctor (transformation of fatty bodies into fat acids and glycerine). Factors relevant to the analysis: (1) particularity vs generality of the transformation (more particular favors eligibility); (2) degree to which the recited article is particular (generic recitation less likely to provide significantly more); (3) nature/extent of change in state or thing (different function/use favors eligibility; mere location change does not); (4) nature of the article transformed (physical/tangible transformations weigh more than intangible/mental); (5) whether transformation is extra-solution activity or field-of-use (transformations that are nominal/insignificant do not provide significantly more). See Gottschalk v. Benson, Diamond v. Diehr, and Mayo discussions; consult MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2B, evaluate whether additional element(s) beyond a judicial exception are well-understood, routine, and conventional activities previously known in the industry; if so (and recited at a high level of generality), they do not amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an additional element (or combination) is specific and unconventional — e.g., confines the claim to a particular useful application of the exception — it favors eligibility (example: DDR Holdings where claims modified conventional hyperlink protocol to dynamically produce a hybrid webpage). If additional elements are merely known and conventional (example: Mayo — measuring metabolite levels by any known process), they do not provide an inventive concept. This consideration overlaps with other Step 2B factors (improvement consideration, mere instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity); evaluate them together. Important points: (a) an element known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine for eligibility purposes (novelty/obviousness is distinct from eligibility); (b) improvements over conventional functionality may support eligibility even if not novel (Enfish discussion). Use case law (DDR, Mayo, Parker v. Flook) and MPEP §2106.05(d) guidance when applying this factor.
